idiom_name: hand-rolled stage loop over an array (function pointer + void* context)
implementation_notes: C has no closures and no generic collection type, so the classic structure can only be hand-written: an array of a concrete element type, one loop per stage, and a function pointer with a void* user_data/context payload to carry what a lambda would capture - the shape the C standard library itself uses for qsort (the bounds-checked C11 qsort_s adds such a context parameter). Callback iteration over containers is a library feature, not a language one: GLib's g_ptr_array_foreach(array, func, user_data) calls a GFunc per element. What replaces the classic structure is therefore an ordinary indexed for loop, which is shorter, type-safe and debuggable; keep the function-pointer form only for genuinely data-driven stage lists (an array of stage descriptors) or where a third-party container API forces callbacks.
pitfalls: void* user_data erases the element type: a single wrong cast inside a stage is a silent memory error, and the compiler checks nothing across stage boundaries.
Every stage has to allocate - and later free - its own output array, so intermediate-collection ownership becomes the bug-prone part of the 'pipeline'.
A callback cannot outlive its context: a stack-allocated context passed by pointer into a deferred or asynchronous stage dangles.
alternative: Prefer an explicit indexed for loop (or one small helper per stage). The pattern's own author documents this rule: without good language support for clean lambdas the pattern 'usually ends up being more trouble than is worth it', and C offers neither closures nor a generic collection abstraction.
